title: KC Documentation
bodyHtml:
This page provides more details on the methods used to produce the knowledge represented on the KC.

Categorization of DCCs by research context

To categorize the relevance of the data produced by the DCCs to the four research contexts that we have defined, we first used a Large Language Model (LLM). We supplied as input a file listing the names and URLs of 12 DCCs. The prompt for the model was as follows:

  1. inspect the list and find all 12 DCCs.
  2. consider the following fields of research: a. Experimental Biology, b. Genetics, c. Drug Development, and d. Computational Biology
  3. for each field of research, using your knowledge and any information you can acquire from the internet, you will generate a ranked order list of all 12 DCCs in terms of their relevance to that field of research. For each list, include the following columns:
    1. "DCC", the DCC short name
    2. "Relevance", the DCC's relevance to the current fields of research (from High, Medium, Low)
    3. "Rationale", a reason as to why that DCC is ranked the way it is
    4. "Utility", a brief explanation of how a researcher in this field can use the DCC's data and tools to aid their work.
  4. for each list, write a short rationale for your criteria on how "high", "medium", "low" relevance scores were judged.

We then reviewed the categorizations and edited them as necessary based on our scientific judgment.

IDG results

In the current version of the KC, we have imported curated results directly from IDG for display on the KC.

On the Gene page, we display IDG's Target Development Level (TDL) classification, which summarizes the amount of evidence supporting this gene as a potential drug target. The classifications are as follows:

  • Tclin: targets of approved drugs
  • Tchem: proteins that bind small molecules with high potency
  • Tbio: proteins with Gene Ontology annotations based on experimental evidence or that meet 2 of the following 3 conditions:
    • mentioned in >5 publications
    • ≥3 NCBI GeneRIF annotations
    • ≥50 commercial antibodies, as counted in the Antibodypedia portal
  • Tdark: no clinical, chemical, or biological links to disease

On the Disease page, we display potential drug targets for the disease being viewed, drawn from a variety of sources by IDG. For more details, see Kelleher et al., 2023.

Curation of 4D Nucleome data

Knowledge generated by our analysis of 4DN data is represented on the KC Gene and Disease pages.

We reviewed 235 human Hi-C sequencing datasets from 4DN that included contact matrix information. Experiment types included in situ Hi-C, Micro-C, Dilution Hi-C, DNase Hi-C, and tethered conformation capture (TCC). We used HiCCUPS (Hi-C computational unbiased peak search) within the cooltools software package to call loops in contact maps. Loop calling was successful for 180 datasets. Using an internal pipeline, we then predicted the coordinates of genomic regions that contact the promoters of specific genes. The coordinates, originally in the GRCh38 genome build, were then lifted over to the GRCh37 genome build (hg19). The target gene link annotation file sets for both genome builds are available at the Common Metabolic Diseases Genome Atlas.

Using genetic association results from the Association to Function Knowledge Portal, we then considered all variants located within the annotated regions that had a positive posterior probability of association with a disease. The sum of the posterior probabilities of variants within an annotated region represents the probability that the gene associated with that region by the Hi-C results is linked to a causal variant for the genetically associated disease.

On the KC Gene page, view results from 4DN by selecting a tissue from the drop-down menu and clicking Search. The plot y-axis shows the sum of posterior probability of association (PPA) for all variants in credible sets or LD clumps within a region annotated as contacting the promoter of the gene being viewed. Disease-variant-tissue links for this gene are grouped along the x-axis by disease. The higher the total PPA, the greater the likelihood that the 3-dimensional contact with the promoter of this gene impacts its tissue-specific regulation and this impact has consequences for disease risk.

On the KC Disease page, view results from 4DN by selecting a tissue from the drop-down menu and clicking Search. The plot shows LD-clumped genetic association signals that are likely to be proximal in 3-dimensional space to the promoter of the indicated gene. The plot y-axis shows the sum of posterior probability of association (PPA) and the x-axis shows the location by chromosome of the lead SNP. Since the table lists independent genetic association signals and there may be more than one independent signal near a gene, some genes may be listed more than once in the table.

Curation of exRNA data

Knowledge generated by our analysis of exRNA data is represented on the KC Gene and Protein pages.

We downloaded files from exrna-atlas.org containing read counts of extracellular RNA (exRNA) fragments carried by RNA binding proteins (RBPs), and matched the sequences of these fragments to protein coding genes in Gencode v19. For each gene, we then calculated the total count of fragments associated with each RBP. More details about the exRNA analysis of associations between exRNAs and RBPs are available in the publication from LaPlante et al., 2023.

On the KC Gene page, results from exRNA are displayed in a plot and table (see an example) for genes from which exRNAs were detected. Read counts of exRNAs originating from the gene of the page are shown, with the RBPs to which they are predicted to bind, in the HepG2 or K562 cell lines or in both cell lines.

On the KC Protein pages for RNA-binding proteins (see an example), the plot and table display genes whose exRNAs are predicted to bind to that RBP, along with read counts and cell lines.

Curation of GTEx data

Knowledge generated by our analysis of GTEx data is represented on the KC Gene and Disease pages.

The t-statistic (T-stat) is a measure of the tissue specificity of gene expression: higher T-stat values indicate greater tissue specificity. We obtained T-stat values from a previous study (Finucane et al., 2018); we plan to recompute these in the future based on the latest GTEx release.

Briefly, to calculate a T-stat, for each gene g and each biosample b a linear regression y ~ x is run across all GTEx samples, with y equal to the expression level of the sample and x equal to an indicator variable that is 1 if the sample has biosample b and 0 if the sample has a biosample from a different tissue. Biosamples in the same tissue as b (but not the same biosample as b) are ignored from the regression.

The resulting t-stat measures the significance of the regression coefficient. Intuitively, the stronger the regression coefficient, the more the biosample predicts high levels of expression, and hence the more specific expression of the gene is to that biosample.

On the KC Gene page, the GTEx: Tissue specificity tab displays T-stat values for the gene being viewed, in biosamples (tissue and cell types) that are grouped into broader tissue categories such as "blood". The GTEx: Gene expression levels tab shows absolute gene expression values across biosamples for the gene being viewed. Gene expression values are originally from GTEx and were loaded to the KC from the Common Metabolic Diseases Genome Atlas (CMDGA). The Dataset column in the table displays the CMDGA accession numbers of the datasets that are linked to their records at CMDGA.

On the KC Disease page, the plot and table on the GTEx card display enrichment of genetic associations within regions near genes with the most tissue-specific expression. These values are computed by applying Stratified LD-score regression (see details) to the GTEx t-stat values and genetic associations from the Association to Function Knowledge Portal. These results represent the degree to which genetic associations for the disease being viewed act through each tissue.

Curation of LINCS data

Knowledge generated by our analysis of LINCS data is represented on KC Gene pages.

We downloaded LINCS L1000 Consensus Signatures from the SigComLINCS website and computed correlations across the L1000 signatures for every pair of perturbations.

On the KC Gene page, the correlation results are shown in a plot and table (see an example) displaying the name of the gene whose signature is correlated to that of the gene of the page, the correlation value, and the perturbation source (CRISPR knockdown or compound treatment).

Curation of Metabolomics Workbench data

Knowledge generated by our analysis of Metabolomics Workbench data is represented on the KC Disease pages.

We reviewed the datasets available in Metabolomics Workbench and selected those whose metadata included an association with disease. After mapping the disease annotations to the Mondo disease ontology, we collected all metabolites with ANOVA analyses in case/control studies. We then identified significant metabolites using Fisher's meta-analysis method.

On the KC Disease page, the plot shows the p-value for significance of association of metabolites with the disease being viewed (x-axis) and metabolites are ordered along the y-axis by decreasing significance. Metabolite names are linked to their records in the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB).
